views.name: cleaned_weekly_sales_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  week_date_formatted AS week_date_formatted,
  week_date AS week_date,
  region AS region,
  platform AS platform,
  segment AS segment,
  customer_type AS customer_type,
  transactions AS transactions,
  sales AS sales,
  week_number AS week_number,
  month_number AS month_number,
  calendar_year AS calendar_year,
  age_band AS age_band,
  demographic AS demographic,
  avg_transaction AS avg_transaction
FROM cleaned_weekly_sales

params.when_to_use: Questions about weekly-level sales metrics broken down by week_date_formatted (a week-level date label), region, platform, segment, and customer_type — e.g., “What were transactions and sales per week by region and platform?” | Analyses that need both raw counts (transactions) and monetary totals (sales) and the derived avg_transaction at the same weekly/region/platform/segment/customer_type grain. | Time-series or cohort comparisons aligned to week_date or week_number/month_number/calendar_year where the weekly period is the intended aggregation unit. | Filtering or slicing by demographic fields available here (age_band, demographic) while keeping results at the weekly × region × platform × segment × customer_type grain.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need a different grain than week × region × platform × segment × customer_type — using this view and then aggregating further can silently miscount averages or per-entity metrics (e.g., avg_transaction stored here is already an average at this view's grain; re-averaging without weighting by transactions will produce wrong results). | When you need row-level transactions or user-level detail (this view is normalized to weekly aggregates). Using it to compute per-customer statistics or deduplicate events will be incorrect because individual events/customers are not present. | When constructing cohorts defined by event timestamps inside the week (e.g., ‘customers active in a specific day within a week’) — the weekly aggregation loses day-level timing and will over/under-count membership for day-level cohorts. | When you need metrics across a different segmentation dimension not present here (for example product category) — joining or re-aggregating expecting product-level fidelity will produce wrong counts because the source rows are already aggregated at the view grain. | When you need canonical price/time series for Bitcoin or other external reference data — this view contains sales/transactions for customers, not market price series; mixing them risks misinterpretation of units and granularity.
params.comparison: use weekly_sales_base instead when you need a sibling view focused on the same weekly sales domain but possibly different column set — it likely provides similar weekly metrics and may be preferable if you want a different set of native aggregations or naming conventions (same domain/likely same grain). | use customer_transactions_by_customer instead when you need per-customer (customer-level) aggregation rather than weekly × region × platform × segment × customer_type — that sibling has customer-grain aggregates (different grain) so it avoids the risk of mis-counting when back-calculating per-customer metrics from weekly aggregates. | use interest_monthly_metrics when you need monthly-level aggregates — this view is aggregated to month (different temporal grain) so it avoids errors from naively summing or averaging weekly rows to represent months without proper calendar alignment or weighting. | use bitcoin_prices_clean when you specifically require clean time-series of Bitcoin prices (different domain and grain) — do not reuse sales fields from this view for market-price analyses. | use shopping_cart_user_events or veg_transactions_with_category when you require event- or product-level detail for joins that need item-level granularity — those siblings are JOIN/event-level and will preserve row-level fidelity that this weekly aggregate does not.

views.description: Normalized projection of cleaned_weekly_sales exposing canonical date parts and preserving all descriptive columns and measures. Parses/aliases primary date and keeps calendar_year/week_number/month_number for easy time-based grouping. Use when asking time-series or dimensional breakdowns of weekly sales. | Use for: time-series of sales/transactions by region/platform/segment/customer_type; monthly or weekly aggregates and growth calculations; demographic or age_band performance comparisons; average transaction analyses and segmentation

views.name: weekly_sales_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  week_date AS week_date,
  region AS region,
  platform AS platform,
  segment AS segment,
  customer_type AS customer_type,
  transactions AS transactions,
  sales AS sales
FROM weekly_sales

params.when_to_use: When you need weekly-level metrics broken down by week_date, region, platform, segment, and customer_type — e.g., “What were transactions and sales by each week, region, platform, segment, and customer_type?” | When you need raw (non-aggregated beyond the listed grain) weekly transactions and sales that are already stored at the exact grain provided (no further grouping required). | When you want a direct pass-through of the underlying weekly_sales table values for downstream joins or filters that preserve the same grain (week_date × region × platform × segment × customer_type). | When building dashboards or reports that present time-series by week and the other four dimensions exactly as columns in this view.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need a different aggregation level (daily, monthly, customer-level, or total across regions/platforms). This view is at the five-dimension weekly grain; aggregating it without care may double-count or hide missing combinations. | Do not use for customer-level analyses (e.g., per-customer lifetime value or per-customer transaction counts). The view has no customer identifier; using it for per-customer metrics will be silently wrong because customer-level detail is absent. | Do not use when you need event-level or cart-event detail (e.g., individual cart events, event timestamps). This view contains only pre-aggregated transactions and sales per week/region/platform/segment/customer_type. | Do not use when you need cohort analyses defined by attributes not present here (e.g., cohort by signup_date or user_id). Cohort membership cannot be derived from the columns present and will lead to incorrect cohorts. | Do not use when you must ensure deduplication of transactions at a lower level (e.g., deduping by transaction_id). The view provides aggregated counts labeled transactions but does not expose identifiers to validate or deduplicate underlying events. | Do not use when comparing different aggregation semantics (e.g., unique users vs. raw transactions). The meaning of transactions here is inherited from weekly_sales; assuming it equals 'unique users' or another metric will produce incorrect conclusions.
params.comparison: use cleaned_weekly_sales_base instead when you need the same weekly grain but with cleaned/normalized source data — it has the same grain (week_date × region × platform × segment × customer_type) but applies source cleaning steps that weekly_sales_base does not. | use customer_transactions_by_customer instead when you need customer-level aggregations — that sibling is aggregated at the customer grain (per-customer totals) whereas weekly_sales_base is aggregated by week and dimension combinations. | use interest_monthly_metrics instead when you need monthly aggregation or finance-specific monthly metrics — it aggregates to month-level and computes metrics not available in weekly_sales_base. | use shopping_cart_user_events or veg_transactions_with_category when you need event- or transaction-level detail or category enrichment — those siblings are JOIN views that expose lower-level event/transaction attributes needed for event-sequence or category analyses, unlike weekly_sales_base which only exposes weekly aggregates. | use bitcoin_member_transactions when analyzing member-level bitcoin transactions — that JOIN view exposes transaction-level bitcoin/member identifiers and semantics that weekly_sales_base does not. | use bitcoin_prices_clean when you need normalized price/time series data for bitcoin (price/time grain) — weekly_sales_base does not contain price history or time-series for bitcoin. | use shopping_cart_event_types when you need canonical event type definitions or a selection of event types — that normalized selection differs in purpose and grain from weekly_sales_base which supplies aggregated sales/transactions.

views.description: Projection of weekly_sales preserving original raw week_date text and all dimension/measure columns. Use when working with the raw weekly_sales fact (pre-cleaning) or comparing raw vs cleaned datasets. | Use for: raw weekly sales trends; data quality comparisons with cleaned_weekly_sales; dimension-level aggregates on raw data

views.name: shopping_cart_user_events
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  e.visit_id AS visit_id,
  e.cookie_id AS cookie_id,
  u.user_id AS user_id,
  e.page_id AS page_id,
  p.page_name AS page_name,
  p.product_category AS product_category,
  p.product_id AS product_id,
  e.event_type AS event_type,
  e.sequence_number AS sequence_number,
  e.event_time AS event_time
FROM shopping_cart_events e
LEFT JOIN shopping_cart_page_hierarchy p ON e.page_id = p.page_id
LEFT JOIN shopping_cart_users u ON e.cookie_id = u.cookie_id

params.when_to_use: Find individual event-level records for a shopping session: questions that need one row per event occurrence within a visit (e.g., 'list all events for visit 123 ordered by sequence_number'). | Join event-level attributes (event_type, event_time, sequence_number) with page metadata and optional user id inferred from cookie: troubleshooting event sequences, reconstructing clickstreams, or building per-event features. | Filter or count events at the visit+sequence granularity (e.g., 'how many add_to_cart events occurred in visit X' or 'what was the nth event in each visit'). | Build higher-level aggregates where the base grain is the event (you will explicitly aggregate by visit_id or user_id as needed).
params.when_not_to_use: When you need one row per visit (session-level metrics) — WHY: the view is at the event grain (visit_id, sequence_number). Reusing it without aggregating will double-count visits and produce too-many rows. | When you need one row per user or per cookie across multiple visits — WHY: the view contains events tied to visits; multiple visits and many events per user exist, so counts/metrics per user require explicit aggregation and deduplication. | When you need deduplicated product- or page-level catalogs (one row per product_id or page_id) — WHY: the view repeats page/product info for every event, so using it as a catalog will lead to duplicated entries unless you SELECT DISTINCT or aggregate. | When you expect complete user identity for every event: cookie->user join is LEFT JOIN and may be NULL — WHY: user_id is populated only when there is a matching cookie in shopping_cart_users; treating user_id as always-present will silently miss anonymous events. | When you need events restricted to pages guaranteed present in page hierarchy: page fields come from a LEFT JOIN to shopping_cart_page_hierarchy and may be NULL — WHY: missing page rows will produce NULL page_name/product_category; queries assuming not-NULL will be incorrect. | When you need pre-aggregated metrics (counts, sums, rates) at any higher aggregation level — WHY: this view is unaggregated; reusing it as if it already produced aggregates will inflate metrics unless you aggregate explicitly. | When you rely on a particular ordering (e.g., first/last event) without using sequence_number properly — WHY: the stored grain includes sequence_number but the view does not enforce uniqueness beyond (visit_id, sequence_number) and does not guarantee monotonicity across visits; assumptions about global ordering or uniqueness across visits are unsafe.
params.comparison: use shopping_cart_event_types(NORM) instead when you only need the event_type reference list — it is a normalized/catalog view of event types and avoids event-level duplication. | use shopping_campaign_active_windows(SEL) instead when you need campaign/window membership for visits — it selects campaign windows rather than returning every event; for campaign-level joins prefer that view to avoid event-level amplification. | use veg_transactions_with_category(JOIN) or customer_transactions_by_customer(AGG) when you need transaction- or customer-level aggregates — these siblings provide pre-joined or aggregated results at an appropriate higher grain, avoiding manual aggregation from per-event rows. | use weekly_sales_base(NORM) or cleaned_weekly_sales_base(NORM) when you need cleaned, normalized sales metrics aggregated by time period — those siblings are normalized/aggregated for period-level queries and do not require you to aggregate raw events. | use bitcoin_member_transactions(JOIN) or bitcoin_prices_clean(NORM) only for unrelated financial/time-series data — these siblings differ in domain and grain; do not substitute this event-level view when domain/context differs.

views.description: Denormalized event-level relation joining shopping_cart_events to shopping_cart_page_hierarchy and shopping_cart_users (via cookie_id) to provide event context (page, product) and user identifier. Useful for funnel, session, and event-sequence analyses. | Use for: session funnel analyses (page sequences leading to conversion); event counts by page_name or product_category; joining events to users for retention/cohort studies

views.name: bitcoin_member_transactions
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  t.txn_id AS txn_id,
  t.member_id AS member_id,
  m.first_name AS first_name,
  m.region AS region,
  t.ticker AS ticker,
  t.txn_date AS txn_date,
  t.txn_time AS txn_time,
  t.txn_type AS txn_type,
  t.quantity AS quantity,
  t.percentage_fee AS percentage_fee
FROM bitcoin_transactions t
LEFT JOIN bitcoin_members m ON t.member_id = m.member_id

params.when_to_use: When you need a row-level (per txn_id) record of bitcoin transactions enriched with the member's demographic fields (first_name, region) — e.g., "list all transactions with member name and region". | When you want to filter, sort or analyze individual transactions by time/date, ticker, txn_type, quantity, or percentage_fee (examples: recent buys/sells per transaction, transaction-level joins to other txn-level tables). | When you need to produce transaction-level inputs for downstream per-transaction processing (per-row ML scoring, exporting raw transactions, or computing custom aggregates where you will explicitly aggregate by txn_id).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute member-level aggregates (totals, averages per member) without first aggregating by member_id — WHY: grain is txn_id (one row per transaction). Reusing it as if one row = one member will double-count members with multiple transactions. | Do not use this view for time-windowed aggregates that assume one row per time bucket per member (e.g., weekly active members) — WHY: it contains multiple txn rows per member per period; you must deduplicate or aggregate to the target grain to avoid inflated counts. | Do not use this view as a source for cohort membership (e.g., "members who transacted in month X") unless you explicitly collapse to distinct member_id for the cohort — WHY: JOIN preserves transaction-level multiplicity so cohort counts will be transaction-counted, not user-counted. | Do not use this view to compute price/time series for tickers (e.g., OHLC per day) — WHY: it contains transaction events, not cleaned or resampled price series; bitcoin_prices_clean is the intended normalized price source. | Do not use this view expecting percent_fee already aggregated or normalized across transactions (e.g., average fee per member) — WHY: percentage_fee is per transaction and must be aggregated correctly (weighted/unweighted) depending on the question. | Do not assume completeness of member attributes: LEFT JOIN to bitcoin_members means transactions without a matching member will still appear with NULL member fields — WHY: silently introduces NULLs for member-derived filters unless you enforce INNER JOIN or filter NULLs explicitly.
params.comparison: use bitcoin_prices_clean instead when you need normalized price/time series or market reference data — it provides price-level cleaning and is the correct source for time-series price analysis, whereas bitcoin_member_transactions is transaction event data. | use customer_transactions_by_customer instead when you want pre-aggregated customer-level metrics (totals, counts, averages) — it has customer/customer-grain aggregates so you don't have to aggregate txn-level rows yourself. | use veg_transactions_with_category instead when you need transaction-level data enriched with categorical product info — it is a JOIN view similar in pattern but focused on product categorization; bitcoin_member_transactions is focused on member enrichment for bitcoin txns. | use cleaned_weekly_sales_base or weekly_sales_base for normalized weekly sales aggregates or sales-specific cleaning (NORM) — those siblings are appropriate when the analysis requires weekly aggregation/normalization rather than raw transaction rows. | use shopping_cart_user_events or shopping_cart_event_types for event-stream style analyses of user shopping behavior — they are event-focused sibling views; bitcoin_member_transactions should be used when the subject is bitcoin transaction rows enriched with member info.

views.description: Event-level join of bitcoin_transactions to bitcoin_members to attach member attributes (first_name, region) to each transaction. Useful for member-level activity, geographic breakdowns, and linking to external user identifiers if available. | Use for: member-level crypto trading volume and fee analysis; geographic distribution of transactions; join to price series by ticker/date for P&L

views.name: interest_monthly_metrics
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  month_year AS month_year,
  _month AS _month,
  _year AS _year,
  COUNT(interest_id) AS interest_id_count,
  AVG(composition) AS avg_composition,
  AVG(index_value) AS avg_index_value
FROM interest_metrics
GROUP BY month_year, _month, _year

params.when_to_use: When you need month-level (calendar month) aggregated metrics for the entire dataset represented by interest_metrics — e.g., “How many distinct interest_id rows appear in each month?” or “What was the average composition and average index_value in each month across all interest_metrics rows?” | When you want simple per-month summaries where each output row represents a single month (identified by month_year, plus numeric _month and _year) and the aggregates are COUNT(interest_id) and simple averages (AVG(composition), AVG(index_value)). | When downstream code expects straightforward SQL-aggregates computed at the month level (no additional filtering by cohort or deduplication logic required).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse this view when you need a different aggregation grain (e.g., per-day, per-week, per-interest, or per-customer). Reason: this view is aggregated to month_year; further aggregating or joining on a finer grain will produce incorrect counts/averages because row-level detail is not preserved. | Do not reuse it to compute distinct counts of interests or unique users across months when de-duplication is required. Reason: the view uses COUNT(interest_id) which counts rows, not DISTINCT interest identifiers; if interest_id repeats within a month you will overcount. | Do not reuse when you need cohorted or filtered metrics (for example: first-time interests in a month, a filtered subset of interest_metrics by attribute, or metrics for a particular segment). Reason: the view contains unfiltered global aggregates; applying filters after aggregation can produce incorrect percentages or miss intended cohort boundaries. | Do not reuse when you need aggregations that depend on row-level weighting or custom aggregation functions (e.g., SUM of weights, weighted average, median). Reason: only unweighted AVG(...) and COUNT(...) are provided; weighted or non-linear aggregations cannot be reconstructed accurately from these columns. | Do not reuse when you need reliable denominators for rate calculations that depend on distinct entities (e.g., ratio of unique interests to active users). Reason: interest_id_count is a raw COUNT; it does not guarantee uniqueness or represent distinct active users. | Do not reuse if you need exact null-handling or to know how many rows contributed to each average (e.g., to compute combined averages across months accounting for differing row counts). Reason: the view exposes AVG(...) but does not expose the underlying counts per averaged column (only COUNT(interest_id)), so reconstructing correct weighted averages across months may be wrong if NULLs or variable row counts exist.
params.comparison: use cleaned_weekly_sales_base(NORM) instead when you need week-level normalized sales data — it has a weekly grain and normalization steps, whereas interest_monthly_metrics is monthly and performs simple aggregation. | use weekly_sales_base(NORM) instead when you need weekly (not monthly) aggregates or the ability to align on week-based time windows — interest_monthly_metrics aggregates to calendar months and cannot represent weekly patterns. | use shopping_cart_user_events(JOIN) instead when you need event-level joins or richer per-user/per-event detail — that sibling preserves row-level event detail while interest_monthly_metrics is pre-aggregated and loses row-level information. | use bitcoin_member_transactions(JOIN) or veg_transactions_with_category(JOIN) when you need join-enriched transaction-level data (category/member/customer attributes) to define cohorts or filters before aggregation — interest_monthly_metrics lacks those join-enriched dimensions. | use customer_transactions_by_customer(AGG) when you require per-customer aggregations (customer-level grain) rather than per-month aggregates — interest_monthly_metrics is per-month and cannot substitute for per-customer metrics. | use bitcoin_prices_clean(NORM) when you require normalized price/time series at a finer resolution or cleaned numeric series — interest_monthly_metrics provides only monthly aggregated averages of index_value and composition, not cleaned time-series price data. | use shopping_campaign_active_windows(SEL) or shopping_cart_event_types(NORM) when you need campaign/window event definitions or normalized event-type dimensions to filter/segment prior to aggregation — interest_monthly_metrics contains only the final month-level metrics and lacks those segmentation helpers.

views.description: Monthly aggregated interest metrics per month_year that summarizes count of interest_id observations and average index/composition values. Useful for trend detection and month-level comparisons across interests. | Use for: monthly trends in interest composition/index; seasonal comparisons across years; identifying months with many active interests

views.name: customer_transactions_by_customer
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id AS customer_id,
  COUNT(*) AS txn_count,
  SUM(txn_amount) AS total_txn_amount,
  MIN(txn_date) AS first_txn_date,
  MAX(txn_date) AS last_txn_date
FROM customer_transactions
GROUP BY customer_id

params.when_to_use: Count and sum transaction-level activity aggregated to the customer level (one row per customer). Use when you need each customer's total number of transactions, total transaction amount, and their first/last transaction dates across the entire customer_transactions table. | Customer-level summary for joins where the downstream logic expects a single row per customer (e.g., enriching a customer dimension with lifetime txn metrics). | Reporting or modeling features that require easy access to per-customer aggregates (txn_count, total_txn_amount) without additional grouping.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need a different grain (e.g., per-transaction, per-day, per-week, per-product). This view is pre-aggregated to customer_id; joining it where the consumer expects transaction rows or time-series rows will silently undercount and collapse multiple transactions into one row. | Do not use for cohort or time-windowed metrics (e.g., transactions within a specific date range such as last 30 days) unless you first filter customer_transactions by that window. The view aggregates over all rows in customer_transactions, so it will produce lifetime totals and earliest/latest dates that do not respect downstream time filters. | Do not use when you need distinct counts on a different attribute (e.g., distinct order_id, distinct session_id) — COUNT(*) here counts rows in customer_transactions, which may not equal distinct counts of other identifiers. | Do not use when you need granular date-based aggregates (e.g., first/last transaction per month) because first_txn_date/last_txn_date are computed across the whole table and will not reflect per-period minima/maxima. | Do not use if your definition of a customer differs from customer_id in customer_transactions (e.g., deduplicated customers table, merged customer identifiers). The view uses customer_transactions.customer_id as-is and will be incorrect if downstream expects reconciled customer identities.
params.comparison: use cleaned_weekly_sales_base instead when you need transaction or sales data normalized and cleaned at a weekly grain — cleaned_weekly_sales_base is a normalization (NORM) view and is likely designed for time-windowed/week-level analysis rather than lifetime per-customer aggregates. | use weekly_sales_base instead when you need pre-aggregated sales by week or time period — weekly_sales_base (NORM) provides time-bucketed aggregation instead of customer-level lifetime aggregation. | use shopping_cart_user_events instead when you need event-level shopping cart interactions (JOIN) or to analyze sequences of user events; that view preserves event rows rather than collapsing to one row per customer. | use veg_transactions_with_category instead when you need transaction rows enriched with product/category information (JOIN). That view keeps per-transaction detail and adds category context that is lost by aggregating to customer level. | use interest_monthly_metrics instead when you need periodic/metric-level aggregation (AGG) by month or interest-specific cohorts — interest_monthly_metrics aggregates over a different dimension and time window, appropriate for monthly trend analysis rather than lifetime customer totals. | use bitcoin_member_transactions instead when analyzing member transactions in the bitcoin domain (JOIN) or when you need domain-specific joins/filters that customer_transactions does not include. | use bitcoin_prices_clean when you need price/reference time-series data (NORM) rather than customer-level transactional aggregates. | use shopping_campaign_active_windows or shopping_cart_event_types when you need campaign/window or event-type metadata (SEL/NORM) to apply filters before aggregating; those views help define cohorts/filters that should be applied to customer_transactions prior to aggregation rather than replacing this customer-level aggregation.

views.description: Customer-level aggregated transactions summarizing total txn_amount, count of transactions, first and last txn_date. Useful for customer lifetime, recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) analyses. | Use for: customer lifetime value and frequency analyses; recency and tenure cohorts; identifying high-value customers

views.name: bitcoin_prices_clean
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ticker AS ticker,
  market_date AS market_date,
  price AS price,
  open AS open,
  high AS high,
  low AS low,
  volume AS volume,
  change AS change
FROM bitcoin_prices

params.when_to_use: Get the daily (per market_date) price and basic trading fields for a specific ticker — e.g., 'What was BTC price, open, high, low, volume, change on 2021-09-01?' | Join to other tables at the same grain (ticker + market_date) where each row represents one ticker-day observation — e.g., enriching daily portfolio returns with the matching ticker/day price. | Compute per-day metrics that require the raw daily price fields themselves (price, open, high, low, volume, change) without additional aggregation — e.g., plotting daily price series or computing daily percent change from the provided 'change' column.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need aggregated data over longer periods (weekly, monthly, etc.) — this view is at daily ticker+market_date grain; aggregating without careful grouping can silently double-count volume or miscompute averages if you don't GROUP BY ticker and market_date correctly. | When you need per-user, per-transaction or member-level metrics — the view has no user/member identifiers; joining it to user tables without a clear join key will create row-multiplication and incorrect cohorts. | When you need event-level or cart-level joins (shopping/e-commerce contexts) — sibling views like shopping_cart_user_events and shopping_cart_event_types represent event-level constructs; using bitcoin_prices_clean for those analyses would mismatch cohort/context and produce meaningless results. | When you expect normalized or canonical market identifiers beyond 'ticker' (e.g., exchange-specific price or instrument id) — this view exposes only 'ticker'; assuming uniqueness across markets/exchanges can cause silent merges of distinct instruments. | When you need deduplicated or filtered records (e.g., latest intra-day tick, or only trading days) — this view simply selects from bitcoin_prices and may include duplicate market_date rows per ticker if source contains them; downstream code must handle deduplication or explicit filtering, otherwise counts/aggregates will be wrong. | When you need pre-joined metrics or aggregated summaries (weekly/monthly metrics, member aggregates) — this view is a normalized base (NORM) of raw daily fields, not an AGG or JOIN that already computes higher-level summaries.
params.comparison: use cleaned_weekly_sales_base instead when you need weekly-level aggregates — it provides weekly aggregation (same domain of 'cleaned' data idea) while bitcoin_prices_clean is daily; choosing cleaned_weekly_sales_base avoids writing your own GROUP BY that could mis-aggregate volume or prices. | use weekly_sales_base instead when your question is explicitly about weekly sales totals/metrics — bitcoin_prices_clean is unrelated grain (daily ticker prices) and will not cover retail sales aggregation needs. | use shopping_cart_user_events or shopping_cart_event_types when analyzing user/cart event sequences — those siblings are event-level or type-level for shopping data and include user/cart keys required to avoid cohort multiplication that would occur if you tried to reuse a price-by-day view for event analysis. | use bitcoin_member_transactions when you need member-linked bitcoin transaction records — bitcoin_member_transactions (JOIN) will have member/context keys; bitcoin_prices_clean lacks member identifiers and cannot safely join to produce per-member transaction summaries without risking cross-product row inflation. | use interest_monthly_metrics or customer_transactions_by_customer when your analysis requires aggregated metrics by month or by customer — those AGG views already handle grouping and aggregation semantics appropriate for those questions, preventing common mistakes like averaging volumes across mismatched grains that would happen if you aggregated bitcoin_prices_clean directly. | use veg_transactions_with_category when you require product category enrichment — that JOIN view includes categorical joins needed to avoid manual and error-prone enrichment that can't be derived from bitcoin_prices_clean.

views.description: Projection of bitcoin_prices keeping raw textual fields and numeric price/open/high/low. Leaves volume and change as-is (text) but exposes the core price series for joins. Use before time alignment with transaction dates. | Use for: time-series price joins with bitcoin_transactions; daily OHLC analyses; cleaning volume/change into numeric measures downstream

views.name: veg_transactions_with_category
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  v."index" AS "index",
  v.txn_date AS txn_date,
  v.txn_time AS txn_time,
  v.item_code AS item_code,
  c.item_name AS item_name,
  c.category_code AS category_code,
  c.category_name AS category_name,
  v."qty_sold(kg)" AS "qty_sold(kg)",
  v."unit_selling_px_rmb/kg" AS "unit_selling_px_rmb/kg",
  l."loss_rate_%" AS "loss_rate_%",
  v."sale/return" AS "sale/return",
  v."discount(%)" AS "discount(%)",
  v.day_of_week AS day_of_week
FROM veg_txn_df v
LEFT JOIN veg_cat c ON v.item_code = c.item_code
LEFT JOIN veg_loss_rate_df l ON v.item_code = l.item_code

params.when_to_use: Answering row-level questions about individual vegetable transactions recorded in veg_txn_df where each row is a single transaction line identified by index — e.g., show the txn_date/txn_time, item, category, quantity (kg), unit price, loss rate and flags for a particular transaction index or list of indices. | Filtering or inspecting individual transactions to diagnose data quality or exceptions (missing category, unexpected loss_rate) because the view preserves the original txn grain and joins enrichment attributes (category and loss rate) without aggregating. | Producing detailed transaction-level reports or exporting transaction rows to downstream systems when you need both txn fields and the vendor/category metadata on the same row.
params.when_not_to_use: Use as a source for aggregated metrics (daily/weekly totals, average unit price, total kg sold) — WHY: the view is at transaction-row (index) grain and contains one row per original transaction; summing or averaging directly from it without explicitly grouping may double-count or misrepresent aggregates, especially if there are multiple txn rows per logical sale. | Use to compute unique-customer or cart-level metrics — WHY: there is no customer or cart identifier in this view and the grain is per item-line; reusing it for customer-level cohorts will produce incorrect cohorts and counts. | Use as the definitive truth for item category mapping without handling nulls — WHY: the category fields come from a LEFT JOIN to veg_cat; some transactions may have no match and yield NULL category_code/category_name. Treat unmatched rows explicitly rather than assuming every item has a category. | Use to compute loss-rate-weighted metrics across time without confirming join cardinality — WHY: loss rates are joined from veg_loss_rate_df by item_code via LEFT JOIN; if veg_loss_rate_df contains multiple rows per item_code (or duplicates), the LEFT JOIN will multiply transaction rows leading to inflated quantities/values unless de-duplicated first. | Use to answer time-series questions that require consistent time bucketing (daily/weekly aggregates with missing days) — WHY: this view exposes txn_date and day_of_week but does not fill missing dates or perform time-bucketing; missing days will not be represented and downstream aggregations must handle gaps explicitly.
params.comparison: use cleaned_weekly_sales_base instead when you need pre-aggregated weekly totals or normalized weekly metrics — it is a NORM sibling providing weekly-level aggregation, whereas veg_transactions_with_category is transaction-row level. | use weekly_sales_base instead when you want normalized weekly aggregates across transactions — weekly_sales_base is a NORM aggregate for weekly summaries while this view is row-grain and will require grouping to produce equivalent results. | use customer_transactions_by_customer instead when you need customer-level aggregations/cohorts — that sibling is AGG at customer grain; veg_transactions_with_category lacks customer identifiers and is at transactional line grain. | use veg_txn_df (base table) when you need the raw transaction fields without category or loss-rate enrichment — veg_transactions_with_category LEFT JOINs additional tables and may introduce NULLs or duplicate rows if the joined tables have multiple matches. | use veg_cat directly when you need the canonical category mapping or to validate category metadata — veg_cat is the source of category_name/code; veg_transactions_with_category joins it for convenience but does not guarantee referential integrity or one-to-one mapping. | avoid using shopping_cart_user_events or shopping_cart_event_types as substitutes — those siblings are focused on shopping-cart event semantics (JOIN/NORM) and contain different keys and grain (events, carts) so they are inappropriate when the question is strictly about item-level veg transactions.

views.description: Joins veg_txn_df to veg_cat and veg_loss_rate_df (by item_code) to provide item name, category, and loss rate alongside each transaction. Useful for margin, category-level sales, and loss-adjusted analyses. | Use for: category-level sales and quantity sold; loss-rate adjusted revenue estimates; price and discount impact analyses by category

views.name: shopping_campaign_active_windows
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  campaign_id AS campaign_id,
  products AS products,
  campaign_name AS campaign_name,
  start_date AS start_date,
  end_date AS end_date
FROM shopping_cart_campaign_identifier

params.when_to_use: Find attributes of a campaign (campaign_id) such as its list of products, readable name, and its configured start_date and end_date — i.e., questions that need the campaign-level metadata for each campaign_id. | Join campaign-level metadata onto other tables at the campaign_id grain (for example, to enrich event or sales rows that already exist at campaign_id level) without expecting any additional filtering or aggregation from this view. | Build reports or lookups that need the canonical start_date/end_date window for each campaign_id as defined in shopping_cart_campaign_identifier.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need rows at a finer grain than campaign_id (for example per-product-per-campaign, per-user-per-campaign, per-event). This view has one row per campaign_id and will silently drop multiplicity: joining it to a finer-grained table will not add the missing detail and can cause undercounting or incorrect deduplication. | Do not use this view to compute metrics that require counting events, users, sales, or impressions. The view contains only metadata columns, no event or transaction counts; reusing it as if it were an aggregated metrics table will produce wrong (usually zero or missing) metric values. | Do not use this view to restrict cohorts by anything other than campaign_id, start_date, end_date, campaign_name, or products. The view does not encode per-user or per-time-sliced cohort membership; using it to filter by cohort will likely produce incorrect cohorts. | Do not use this view to infer campaign activity during arbitrary time windows beyond the stored start_date and end_date. The view provides the configured start_date/end_date fields only; it does not contain records of actual activity or verify that activity occurred within those dates. | Do not use this view when you need normalized or cleaned price/transaction data, event types, or time-series metrics — it is purely a direct projection of shopping_cart_campaign_identifier and contains no normalization, aggregation, or enrichment.
params.comparison: use shopping_cart_event_types(NORM) instead when you need canonical event type definitions for joining or filtering — shopping_campaign_active_windows has campaign metadata but contains no event type information. | use veg_transactions_with_category(JOIN) or customer_transactions_by_customer(AGG) instead when you need transaction-level details or aggregated customer transaction metrics — those sibling views contain transaction data or aggregates, while shopping_campaign_active_windows contains only campaign-level metadata. | use cleaned_weekly_sales_base(NORM) or weekly_sales_base(NORM) instead when your question is about time-series sales at weekly grain — those siblings provide sales data at a time grain, whereas this view provides only campaign metadata (no time-series sales). | use shopping_cart_user_events(JOIN) when you need user-level events tied to campaigns — shopping_cart_user_events contains event rows and is appropriate for counting or cohorting users, while shopping_campaign_active_windows is one row per campaign and cannot supply per-user event detail.

views.description: Campaign rows with start/end dates exposed for filtering to active campaigns in a dynamic query. Keeps campaign_id, campaign_name and product list. Use as a base for joining events or transactions to campaigns via date overlaps. | Use for: identify events/transactions that fall within campaign windows; campaign-level performance over their active period

views.name: shopping_cart_event_types
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  event_type AS event_type,
  event_name AS event_name
FROM shopping_cart_event_identifier

params.when_to_use: When you need a canonical list of shopping cart event types and their display names (one row per event_type). | When you want to join on event_type to add human-readable event_name metadata to facts or other dimension tables. | When you need to validate or map raw event_type codes from shopping_cart_event_identifier to their friendly names.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need any metric aggregated at a different grain (for example, counts of events, users, or sessions) — this view has one row per event_type and contains no event-level or user-level rows, so joining it as if it were event data will not produce correct counts. | When you need a filtered cohort (e.g., events within a date range, by user segment, or by campaign) — this view contains no timestamp, user, campaign, or filter columns, so it cannot represent subsets of events and will silently return all event types regardless of cohort. | When you need attributes beyond event_type and event_name (for example pricing, category, or transaction fields) — those columns are not present and must be obtained from other tables; assuming they exist here will cause query errors. | When you expect one-to-many or many-to-many relationships (e.g., multiple names per event_type over time) — this view exposes the current mapping as stored in shopping_cart_event_identifier; it does not encode history or multiplicity, so reuse for temporal name changes will be incorrect. | When you need to rely on referential completeness for events present in an events fact table — this view is a mapping source only and may not imply that every event_type exists in a particular events dataset; joining without outer-join logic may drop rows or misrepresent coverage.
params.comparison: use shopping_cart_user_events instead when you need event-level rows (timestamps, user ids, or counts) — shopping_cart_user_events is a JOIN that contains event occurrences, whereas shopping_cart_event_types is a normalized dimension with one row per event_type. | use cleaned_weekly_sales_base or weekly_sales_base when analyzing sales metrics by time period — those sibling views are normalized/aggregated around sales and time grains, while shopping_cart_event_types provides only type-to-name mapping without temporal or sales data. | use veg_transactions_with_category or bitcoin_member_transactions when you require transactional fields or category/financial details — those JOIN views include transaction-level or enriched attributes that shopping_cart_event_types does not provide. | use interest_monthly_metrics or customer_transactions_by_customer when you need aggregated metrics (monthly or per-customer) — those are AGG views with pre-aggregated measures, unlike this view which has no measures and a different grain (event_type).

views.description: Simple projection of event type mappings to attach human-readable event_name to event_type. Use to decode event_type integers in event-level analyses. | Use for: map event_type to event_name for reporting; join to events to get descriptive event names
